Behavioural phenotypes Which of the following genetic disorders are described in the below scenarios? 1. Amy Patterson is a 6-year-old girl who exhibits repeated hand wringing and marked behavioural disturbance.

2. Jamie Walters is a 10-year-old boy who has severe learning disability but is generally described as happy and laughing much of the time.

3. Kyle Peters is a 9-year-old boy who attends a mainstream primary school. His parents and teachers have noted that he tends to be rather socially awkward and shy. 4. Julie Stevens is a 12-year-old girl who attends a mainstream school with some additional support. She is very outgoing with peers and interacts readily with strangers. Explanation: 1) Children with Rett's syndrome often display repetitive hand-wringing and other hand movements which often occur from early childhood and persist, with some change, into adolescence. 2) Children with Angelman's syndrome have severe intellectual impairment but are highly social with a happy demeanor and often display arm-waving and similar behaviours 3) Fragile X syndrome is characterized by social anxiety, including poor eye contact, gaze aversion, prolonged time to commence social interaction, and challenges forming friendships. Social anxiety is one of the most common features seen, with up to 75% of males in one series characterized as having excessive shyness and 50% having panic attacks. It is thought to be due to impairment of face encoding and recognition. 4) People with William's syndrome usually have mild to moderate intellectual disability with particular problems with visuospatial tasks such as drawing and fewer problems with language. They often have an outgoing personality and interact readily with strangers.

Correct Answer is : 1. Amy Patterson is a 6-year-old girl who exhibits repeated hand wringing and marked behavioural disturbance. - Rett's syndrome 2. Jamie Walters is a 10-year-old boy who has severe learning disability but is generally described as happy and laughing much of the time. - Angelman's syndrome 3. Kyle Peters is a 9-year-old boy who attends a mainstream primary school. His parents and teachers have noted that he tends to be rather socially awkward and shy. - Fragile X syndrome 4. Julie Stevens is a 12-year-old girl who attends a mainstream school with some additional support. She is very outgoing with peers and interacts readily with strangers. - William's syndrome

Childhood disorders Which of the following diagnoses are most appropriate for each of the below scenarios? 1. Her mother has raised concerns with the health visitor that Kate does not seem to respond to aff ection, does not seek out cuddles and seems ambivalent to her presence. She is developing normally otherwise. 2. Colin Eames is a 4-year-old boy who has limited speech. He cannot use sentences and, for example, only uses the word "drink" when he wants water. He becomes very upset when he is away from home, especially in places that are noisy. He does not show much interest in playing with adults or other children. 3. Holly Ward is a 9-year-old girl whose teachers have raised concerns about her. She has a good vocabulary but cannot write sentences of longer than 6 words or read books, which would normally be suitable for children 3-4 years, her junior. She has started to have angry outbursts in class. On interview, she presents as bright and is able to answer your questions clearly. 4. Simon Lovell is a 10-year-old boy who struggles to concentrate at school and becomes upset in loud environments. However, he is happy at home and can produce excellent work at home without diffi culty. 5. Laura Tierney is a 9-year-old girl who is doing well at school and has plenty of friends. However, she is getting upset as she is unable to ride her bike and tie her shoelaces, unlike her peers. Explanation: 1) This is likely to be reactive attachment disorder. This arises from a failure to form normal attachments to primary caregivers in early childhood, often due to early experiences of neglect, abuse, abrupt separation from caregivers between the ages of six months and three years, frequent change of caregivers, or a lack of caregiver responsiveness to a child's communicative eff orts. It is characterised by inappropriate social interactions, which are often inhibited or limited in scope. 2) This is likely to represent an autistic spectrum disorder,

which is characterised by limited language development, impaired social skills and restricted and repetitive interests. 3) This is likely to be dyslexia, characterised by limited reading skills, which then impair writing ability. Her angry outbursts are likely the result of her frustrations over this. 4) This is likely to be an auditory processing disorder in which an individual has diffi culty recognising and interpreting sounds properly. In children this can impair their concentration and lead to them becoming overwhelmed and upset in loud places. 5) This is likely to represent dyspraxia, in which an individual struggles to co-ordinate movements. It can be associated with other developmental disorders but can occur alone. Correct Answer is : 1. Kate Forlock is a 2-year-old girl who was adopted into her current family around 9 months ago. However, she is getting upset as she is unable to ride her bike and tie her shoelaces, unlike her peers. - Dyspraxia

stem: Patterns of genetic inheritance Which of the following patterns of genetic inheritance are associated with the below presentations? 1. Mrs Kerry Arulpragasam is a 40-year-old woman with a long-standing history of benign masses aff ecting her skin and internal organs. She experiences seizures as a consequence of these masses. 2. Miss Holly Wood is a 5-year-old girl with severe intellectual disability and severe self-injurious behaviour, which has required inpatient care. 3. Leo Ximenez is a 7-year-old boy with mild-moderate intellectual disability. His parents are informed that his cognitive diffi culties are due to the most common inherited genetic cause for intellectual impairment. Explanation: 1) This describes tuberous sclerosis, which can be caused by abnormalities in two separate tumour suppressor genes. These can occur spontaneously (more common) or are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. 2) This describes Lesch Nyhan syndrome, which is inherited in a X-linked recessive pattern. 3) Fragile X Syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and is inherited in a X-linked dominant pattern. Correct Answer is : 1. Mrs Kerry Arulpragasam is a 40-year-old woman with a long-standing history of benign masses aff ecting her skin and internal organs. She experiences seizures as a consequence of these masses. - Autosomal dominant 2. Miss Holly Wood is a 5-year-old girl with severe intellectual disability and severe self-injurious behaviour, which has required inpatient care. - X-linked recessive 3. Leo Ximenez is a 7-year-old boy with mild-moderate intellectual disability. His parents are informed that his cognitive diffi culties are due to the most common inherited genetic cause for intellectual impairment. - X-linked dominant

EMI- Variations in cognitive impairment Lead In: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in each of the below scenarios? 1. Mr. Frank Lewis is a 41-year-old man who has presented to his GP with a history of memory decline for several months, unsteady gait and recurrent falls. On examination he had nystagmus, dysarthria and lower limb weakness; his refl exes were absent. His father died in his 30's from a myocardial infarction 2. Mrs. Deborah Banner is a 60-year-old woman with a history of Type 2 diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia. Her husband is concerned, as her memory appears to have declined gradually over a year. He persuades her to go to the GP but she appears unconcerned about his worries. 3. Mr. Charles Rawlins is a 71-year-old man who has been under follow-up with neurology for the last few years for persistent rigidity and tremors. He has now presented with visual hallucinations, that hefi nds distressing, and intermittent confusion.

Explanation: 1) Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus is characterised by dementia, gait ataxia, urinary incontinence, recurrent falls and enlarged cerebral ventricles. It is associated with an increased prevalence of cardiovascular diseases. 2) Binswanger's disease is a form of small vessel vascular dementia caused by damage to the white brain matter. It is characterized by loss of memory and intellectual function and by changes in mood and aff ect. 3) Lewy body dementia is an umbrella term that includes Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), two dementias characterized by abnormal deposits of the protein alpha-synuclein in the brain. Dementia with Lewy bodies is distinguished from Parkinson's disease dementia by the time frame in which dementia symptoms appear relative to parkinsonian symptoms. DLB is diagnosed when cognitive symptoms begin before or at the same time as Parkinsonism, while PDD is the diagnosis when Parkinson's disease is well established before dementia occurs.

Approaches used in psychotherapy Therapists using diff erent models of psychotherapeutic interventions employ distinct approaches to achieve therapeutic benefi ts. For each of the approach listed or described below choose the most likely type(s) of psychotherapy where it is employed, from the below list. 1. Identifying a safe place (Choose ONE) 2. Outside-in approach (Choose ONE) 3. Reformulation (Choose ONE) 4. Rolling with resistance (Choose ONE) 5. Socratic questioning (Choose TWO)

6. Task-setting stage (Choose ONE) 1. Before beginning EMDR therapy, the client is often asked to identify a "safe place". This is usually a comforting memory or an image that gives a positive sense of self. This safe place is used later to help a client tolerate any upsetting sessions and bring closure to them. - 2. Most of the time we complete external actions to match our internal feelings. This is called the “ inside-out ” perspective. As a result, we often want to have motivation or ‘drive’ to precede the completion of a task; in lack there of, we watch Netfl ix! In behavioural activation, patients are expected to act according to a pre-made plan or written goal, so that actions precede – not follow – feeling states. This is called “outside-in” approach to behaviour. 3. In cognitive analytical therapy, following an extended assessment, the therapist and the client develop a joint description of maladaptive

patterns. A diagrammatic ‘reformulation’ is prepared, and enactments are identifi ed both during and outside of the sessions (‘recognition’). New ways of thinking, feeling and behaving are identifi ed as exits from the maladaptive patterns (‘revision’). These 3 Rs are the core features fo Cognitive Analytical Therapy (CAT). 4. Five principles of Motivational Interviewing include (1) Expressing empathy (2) Developing discrepancy between clients' values and their behaviors. (3) Avoiding direct confrontation. (4) Rolling with the resistance from the client instead of abrasively opposing it (5) Supporting self-effi cacy and optimism. 5. The term cognitive restructuring refers to the process of challenging, and changing, irrational thoughts. Socratic questioning is one technique to encourage this. It is used in cognitive therapy as well as CBT. 6. The initial session of Strategic Family Therapy is broken down into 5 parts: the brief social stage (ice-breaking), the problem stage (family members present their main problems), the interactional stage (family members asked to talk to each other to ascertain problems in communication), goal-setting stage (family members asked to list changes they would like to see), andfi nally the task-setting stage (family members given a simple directive to keep involved in between sessions) Ref: 1. Mitrani, V.B., & Perez, M.A. (2003). Structural-strategic approaches to couple and family 31 therapy. In T.L. Sexton, G.R. Weeks, & M.S. Robbins (Eds.), Handbook of family therapy (pp. 177-200). New York: Brunner-Routledge. 2. Clark GI, Egan SJ. The Socratic method in cognitive behavioural therapy: A narrative review. Cognitive Therapy and Research. 2015 Dec 1;39(6):863-79. 3. Curran, J., Ekers, D., McMillan, D., & Houghton, S. (2012). Behavioural activation. In W.Dryden (Ed.), Cognitive behaviour therapies (pp. 236-260). London, UK: Sage Publications. 4. Menon SB, Jayan C. Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing: A conceptual framework. Indian journal of psychological medicine. 2010 Jul;32(2):136. Correct Answer is : Identifying a safe place (Choose ONE) - Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing Outside-in approach (Choose ONE) - Behavioural Activation Therapy Reformulation (Choose ONE) - Cognitive Analytical Therapy Rolling with resistance (Choose ONE) - Motivational Interviewing Socratic questioning (Choose TWO) - Cognitive Therapy, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy Task-setting stage (Choose ONE) - Strategic Family Therapy

stem: Long term eff ects of drugs of abuse Which of the following physiological disturbances are associated with long-term use of the below drugs of abuse? You can use the options more than once. 1. Ketamine 2. Amphetamine 3. Heroin Explanation: 1) Ketamine has been reported as causing renal damage, in addition to its established risk of ulcerative cystitis. 2) Long-term amphetamine use can be associated with hypertension as it is a physiological stimulant. 3) Heroin and other opiates can be associated with a variety of renal complications, including membranous nephropathy, nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis, focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) amyloidosis, and interstitial nephritis. Focal membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with IgM and complement deposition is also found in heroin addicts with the nephrotic syndrome. There is a three-fold increased risk for renal dysfunction in heroin users versus non-drug users. (Ref: Singh, V. P., Singh, N., & Jaggi, A. S. (2013). A Review on Renal Toxicity Profi le of Common Abusive Drugs. The Korean Journal of Physiology & Pharmacology?: Offi cial Journal of the Korean Physiological Society and the Korean Society of Pharmacology, 17(4), 347–357) Correct Answer is : 1. Ketamine - Renal membrane nephropathy 2. Amphetamine - Hypertension 3. Heroin - Renal membrane nephropathy

It can cause: dilated pupils, poor concentration, teeth grinding, problems focusing visually, ataxia, poor short-term memory, hallucinations, delusions and erratic behaviour. 3) Prolonged alcohol use can lead to Wernicke's encephalopathy with features of confusion, ataxia and visual disturbances. Correct Answer is : 1. Mr Majid David is a 32-year-old man who has presented to his local A&E after having the sensation of something crawling under his skin for the last several hours. - Cocaine 2. Event Rates in Clinical Trials Lead In: Which of the following terms best describe the concepts below? 1. Experimental Event Rate- - Control Event Rate 2. 1/ (Experimental Event Rate- Control Event Rate) 3. Proportion of experimental event/proportion of control event Explanation: 1. The absolute arithmetic diff erence in rates of observed outcomes of interest between experimental and control participants in a trial, calculated as |EER - CER| is the risk diff erence. It is also called the ARR or ABI (Absolute Benefi t Increase)= CER (Control Event Rate) – EER (Experimental Event Rate). 2. The Number Needed to Treat (NNT) is the number of patients you need to treat to prevent one additional bad outcome (death, stroke, etc.). To calculate the NNT, you need to know the Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR); the NNT is the inverse of the ARR: NNT = 1/ARR, NNTs are always rounded up to the nearest whole number. 3. The ratio of risk in the treated group (EER) to the risk in the control group (CER) is called Relative Risk or Risk Ratio (RR). This is often used in RCTs and cohort studies and is calculated as EER/CER. Note: An odds ratio (OR) is a measure of association between an exposure and an outcome. The OR represents the odds (not proportions) that an outcome will occur given a particular exposure, compared to the odds of the outcome occurring in the absence of that exposure. Ref: https://ebm-tools.knowledgetranslation.net/resource/glossary

Theme-Neurotic and Somatic Symptom Disorders Lead In: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in each of the scenarios given below? 1. Miss Sylvia Young is a 32-year-old woman who is convinced that she is suff ering from a severe autoimmune disease. She has attended numerous doctors, both within the NHS and in private sector, seeking a diagnosis but has been advised that no sign of an autoimmune disorder can be found. She is very upset with the health system now and continues to be convinced that the doctors are missing a serious health concern. 2. Mr Giles Hardy is a 52-year-old man who is the primary caregiver for his mother with Alzheimer's disease. He has contacted the ambulance service to report developing sudden onset weakness in his right leg. He is admitted urgently to the hospital. A thorough physical examination and investigations done while he was clerked in indicates no evidence of any neurological abnormality.

3. Mr. Philip Crawford is a 27 year old man who believes that his nose is abnormally large. He has had an expensive rhinoplasty arranged privately but remains convinced that his nose is unusually shaped even after the surgical correction. The operating cosmetic surgeon showed him multiple pictures explaining the anatomy of nose in comparison to the pictures of his own nose. Unconvinced, he has now requested another plastic surgery and the surgeon declined this request and referred him to the local mental health team.

Explanation: 1) Hypochondriasis is characterised by the individual being convinced that they are suff ering from a signifi cant illness and then seeking a specifi c diagnosis. They may experience some symptoms, but unlike in somatisation disorder, the focus is more on the diagnosis. 2) Conversion disorder presents with neurological symptoms, such as numbness, blindness, paralysis orfi ts, which are not consistent with a well-established organic cause, which cause signifi cant distress, and can be traced back to a psychological trigger. 3) Body dysmorphic

disorder, or dysmorphophobia, is a mental disorder characterised by the obsessive idea that some aspect of one's own body or appearance is severelyfl awed. Aff ected individuals will attempt to conceal or rectify this perceived abnormality, often via plastic surgery or similar procedures. This does not usually address the problem and they often present again with the same complaint.

The "System for Information on Grey Literature in Europe" (SIGLE) is an European initiative operated by a network of national information or document supply centres active in collecting and promoting grey literature (especially conference abstracts, doctoral thesis etc.). stem: Mr. Owsley is a 60-year-old man who has presented with a number of cognitive impairments and has been diagnosed with a non- degenerative dementia. Which of the following is an example of a non- degenerative dementia?
explanation: Alcoholic dementia is a non-degenerative process as the damage caused ceases once alcohol is no longer being consumed. The other disorders listed are degenerative and progressive. Other examples of non-degenerative dementia include: cancer with or without brain metastases; normal-pressure hydrocephalus; subdural haematoma; hypothyroidism; vitamin B12 defi ciency; and neurosyphilis.

explanation: Donepezil can be associated with bradycardia, heart block and syncope. Heart rate must be monitored when this medication is started and when the dose is increased.

The other disorders listed can be associated with dangerous driving but this is dependent upon the symptoms an individual experience, whether they are experiencing an episode of illness.

stem: Mrs Larkin attends the diagnostic memory clinic with her husband. She is 55 years old and currently working as a teacher but has noticed that she isfi nding it increasingly diffi cult to plan lessons and has lost her confi dence in social situations. Her husband has noticed she is repetitive and is worried because she got lost driving to their holiday house despite usually knowing the route well. What is the most common neurodegenerative disorder in those aged less than 65 years?
explanation: The most common cause of young onset dementia (ie: in those aged 30 - 64) is Alzheimer's disease, followed by vascular, followed by frontotemporal, alcohol related, dementia with Lewy bodies, and Huntington's disease. (Ref: Sampson EL, Warren JD, Rossor MN. Young onset dementia. Postgraduate Medical Journal 2004;80:125-139).

stem: Mrs Jones is a retired science teacher and her husband has recently been diagnosed with dementia. She is interested to know how his dementia is classifi ed. Which of the following dementia is correctly matched with the brain area it aff ects in the initial stages of the disease process?
explanation: Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia are both cortical. Vascular dementia, Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, Huntington's disease, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease and hydrocephalus are sub-cortical. Dementia with Lewy bodies is considered to be cortico- subcortical (Mixed type) (Ref: Shaik, S. S. and Varma, A. R. (2012), Diff erentiating the dementias: a neurological approach. Prog. Neurol. Psychiatry, 16: 11-18. doi:10.1002/pnp.224 http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/pnp.224/pdf)

stem: Mrs Tanya Walters is a 75-year-old woman with an existing diagnosis of mild Alzheimer's dementia. Over the past 5 weeks her family have noticed that she has been persistent low in mood, withdrawn and has shown no interest in activities, which she used to enjoy. On assessment, she expresses feeling “useless” and constantly tired. Which of the following would be the most appropriate management plan at this point?
options: Urine dip and blood tests to exclude organic causes
correctAnswer: Urine dip and blood tests to exclude organic causes
explanation: While patients with dementia can become depressed and require antidepressant medication or other interventions, they are more vulnerable than the general population to developing mood disturbance in response to organic illness, which may not be immediately apparent. It is prudent to check for organic illness before off ering an antidepressant. Remember that MDD is a disorder of exclusion in the elderly. SSRIs are more appropriate than tricyclics in the older population who may have cardiac disease or be on other medications with potential drug interactions.

stem: Mr Benjamin Wyles is a 77-year-old man with a history of recurrent depressive disorder. He is currently experiencing a severe episode of depression and his appetite is very poor. His illness has not responded to 3 adequate trials of antidepressants. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for him at this stage?
explanation: The patient is experiencing a severe treatment resistant episode of depression with marked appetite disturbance. It would be reasonable to treat him with ECT to achieve rapid improvement and address his appetite disturbance while also continuing antidepressants. Older patients can receive ECT and often respond well.

stem: Older people who express suicidal ideation or attempt suicide are at greater future risk than younger patients. Which of the following is most associated with suicide in old age?
explanation: Avoidant and anankastic personality disorder are associated with increased risk of suicide in older people. Histrionic personality disorder is associated with a lower risk of suicide. All personality disorders are associated with an increased risk of suicidal ideation. Male gender, being widowed and having a lower openness to experience are associated with an increased risk of suicide in older age.

stem: Mrs Lisbeth Slander is a 79-year-old woman who has progressively developed loss of memory, visual hallucinations and intermittent irritability over the course of several months. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for her condition?
explanation: This is most likely to represent Lewy Body Dementia, which is characterized by memory impairment, perceptual disturbances and mood changes. Thefi rst line of treatment is acetyl cholinesterase inhibitors, such as Rivastigamine.

stem: Mr Aubrey is a 36-year-old man with a diagnosis of panic disorder. He is unwilling to have talking therapy but is asking about medication options. Which of the following would be most appropriate medication to consider initially for treating panic disorder?
explanation: SSRIs like Sertraline are recommended as thefi rst line medication for panic disorder. Other antidepressants could potentially be used.

stem: Terry is a 43-year-old man with bipolar disorder and is on Lithium treatment. He is now presenting with mixed aff ective state. His recent Lithium level is 0.8. What would be your next step?
explanation: Mixed aff ective state should be treated as manic episode. The best strategy in this situation is to start him on an antipsychotic medication. Li levels are optimal and to increase further could risk toxicity.

stem: Mr. Jameson is a 35-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with ADHD of moderate severity. He is keen to receive treatment due to the impact his symptoms have at his work. Which of the following are recommended as thefi rst line treatment in adult ADHD?
explanation: Medication is the mainstay of treatment for adults with ADHD. Methylphenidate is thefi rst line treatment, with atomoxetine and dexamphetamine being options if this is ineff ective. CBT can be trialled if medication does not show positive eff ects.

stem: Mrs. Kelvin is a 42-year-old woman with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. She has struggled to take her oral medication in the past and has now agreed to have a depot instead. Which of the following depot mediations requires at least 2 hours monitoring after it has been given?
explanation: Patients receiving olanzapine as a depot must be monitored for at least 2 hours after administration. Olanzapine post-injection syndrome has been estimated to occur after 0.07% of olanzapine depot injections and in approximately 1.4% of treated patients. Post-injection syndrome includes a range of signs and symptoms such as sedation and delirium that are consistent with olanzapine overdose. Other symptoms include dizziness, weakness, aggression, ataxia, hypertension and seizures. Extrapyramidal symptoms are also reported, such as tremor, dystonia, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia. It generally starts around 1 hour after administration and resolves after 24-72 hours.

stem: John is a 29-year-old man with a long history of paranoid schizophrenia and recently started on a new antipsychotic medication. His baseline BP was 130/70. During his weekly review, his blood pressure was 160/90. Which of the following antipsychotic drug is most associated with hypertension?
explanation: Most case reports implicate clozapine with some clearly describing normal blood pressure before clozapine was introduced, a sharp rise during treatment and return to normal when clozapine was discontinued. Data available through the committee on safety of medicines yellow card system in the UK indicate that clozapine is the antipsychotic drug most associated with hypertension. There are a small number of reports on Olanzapine, Risperidone, Quetiapine and aripiprazole. (Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines- 11th edition; pg no-122)

stem: Miss Lodge is a 29-year-old woman who has been referred to an outpatient clinic and brought by her family. She receives an MMSE but performs poorly. She was irritable. She states that she has no time to complete the test and that she needs to speak to the Chief Constable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis is an episode of mania in view of the grandiose delusion she describes and irritability with the assessment process. The other diagnoses would be unlikely in a person of this age, unless there was some evidence to support them.

stem: Miss Newton is a 36-year-old woman with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia. She is receiving an optimum medication regime for her and is currently an inpatient in a rehabilitation unit with a view towards reintegrating her into "normal life“. Which of the following will be most likely to help her return to independent living?
explanation: There is signifi cant evidence to indicate that supported employment, particularly Individual Placement and Support, is eff ective in enabling people with chronic psychosis to function more eff ectively in the community.

stem: Mr. Vano is a 24-year-old man who has recently been admitted to a general hospital. Which of the following physical health conditions would be most likely to increase his risk of suicide?
explanation: A history of a traumatic brain injury may increase the subsequent risk of suicide 9-fold. HIV positive status can double the risk of suicide.

stem: Mr Mullen is a 30-year-old soldier who returned from Afghanistan 3 months ago. Towards the end of his tour of duty he witnessed an unexpected attack where his close friend and fellow soldier was shot and killed. He managed to escape but was shot in his left leg in the crossfi re and continues to experience pain. He visits his GP as he is concerned about persistentfl ashbacks of the event and a sense of being on edge all the time. This has been occurring for the last 1 month. Which features would not be consistent with a diagnosis of PTSD?
options: Symptoms occurring within 6 months of the original trauma
explanation: Recurring dreams, diffi culty concentrating and irritability are common features of PTSD. Symptoms typically occur within 6 months (though in delayed onset can occur more than 6 months after the trauma). Hypersomnia is not a common feature in PTSD as the presentation is generally one of hyperarousal.

stem: Miss Saunders is a 25-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, who has been referred to your outpatient clinic by her GP with a likely episode of depression of moderate severity. Which of the following symptoms is she most likely to exhibit?
explanation: Depression and somatoform disorder are highly co-morbid, with around 50% of patients with depression or anxiety having signifi cant somatoform symptoms. Nihilistic delusions or auditory hallucinations would indicate a diagnosis of psychotic depression, which would therefore be severe. Over talkativeness and agitation are more likely in mania or a mixed aff ective episode.

stem: Mr Mathey is a 26-year-old man who has been brought into A&E with fever, confusion, agitation and auditory hallucinations over the last several hours. He has a lumbar puncture as part of his assessment, which demonstrates lymphocytosis, normal glucose and increased protein. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Herpes encephalitis is the most likely diagnosis in view of the acute onset of symptoms suggesting systemic infl ammation and neurological involvement. Patients commonly have marked lymphocytosis, increased red cells, increased protein and low or normal glucose levels in CSF.

stem: Mr Davidson is a 37-year-old man who has a diagnosis of bipolar aff ective disorder and has been admitted to a mental health unit with a mixed aff ective episode. He had discontinued his previous medication. Which of the following treatments would be most appropriate for managing his current episode?
explanation: Valproate has established eff ectiveness in mixed aff ective episodes, as do atypical antipsychotics. Mixed aff ective episodes do not appear to respond well to Lithium, in contrast to its eff ectiveness in classical mania. There is no evidence for Lamotrigine in mania or mixed aff ective episodes.

stem: Mr Harris is a 42-year-old man with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia who is currently stable. He is a heavy smoker and requires a Clozapine dose of 1000mg daily to maintain his serum clozapine level in a therapeutic range. He has been admitted to a general hospital following a generalised seizure in the community. The medical team does not identify any intracranial or systemic cause for his seizure. Which of the following should be done to reduce the risk of further seizure activity?
explanation: In this case, adding sodium valproate would likely be the most appropriate option. It has a broad spectrum of anti-seizure activity and does not have a major impact upon clozapine metabolism. Reducing clozapine dose is an option in some patients but not for this patient as it would likely lead to his serum clozapine level being below the therapeutic range. Carbamazepine induces the enzymes that metabolise clozapine, reducing the serum clozapine level. Adding amisulpride would likely increase the risk of seizure activity, as it will lower the seizure threshold. And if the patient is treatment resistant, they likely require clozapine; changing to an alternative antipsychotic could lead to an increase in psychotic symptoms.

stem: Mrs. Ginner is a 34-year-old woman with a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa. She has been admitted to a general hospital due to concerns about dehydration and profound weight loss. Disturbance of which of the following electrolytes most requires monitoring during the refeeding of profoundly unweight patients?
explanation: While disturbance of all electrolytes can occur in profoundly underweight patients, it is serum phosphate levels that are most important to monitor. Refeeding increases the release of insulin, which requires phosphate, magnesium and potassium. These are usually depleted body- wide. Serum phosphate is also depleted by the formation of phosphate-containing carbohydrate compounds in the muscle and liver. If refeeding is done gradually, these electrolyte disturbances can gradually be corrected. If done too rapidly, the body does not have the time or capacity to respond to the changes in serum electrolytes, leading to profound hypophosphataemia. Cardiac arrhythmias are the most common cause of death from refeeding syndrome, with other signifi cant risks including confusion, coma and convulsions and cardiac failure.

stem: Mr Maloney is a 27-year-old man admitted to the surgical ward following emergency appendectomy. On thefi rst postoperative night, he is seen to be restless and wanting to know if he can leave the ward. When his history is reviewed it is noted he is a heroin user, and usually smokes daily. Which of the following is not an early sign of opiate withdrawal?
explanation: The early signs of opiate withdrawal include agitation, anxiety, muscle aches, increased tearing, insomnia, runny nose, sweating, yawning. Later symptoms of withdrawal include abdominal cramping, diarrhoea, dilated pupils, goose bumps, nausea, vomiting.

stem: Schizophrenia is associated with a variety of clinical symptoms, aside from hallucinations and delusions. This includes cognitive defi cits. Which of the following is most likely to be impaired when people with schizophrenia receive cognitive testing?
explanation: Working memory is most likely to be impaired in schizophrenia. This can have eff ects upon other cognitive functions, such as selective attention and abstract reasoning.

stem: Mrs. Manner is 60-year-old woman who has presented to her GP in a distressed state and reports that she has been experiencing a burning sensation in all her limbs. She is examined and has investigations but no physical cause is found. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is most likely to be somatoform pain disorder, which is characterised by chronic pain that does notfi t with any recognised clinical syndromes or neurological pathways and is often associated with marked psychological distress. Somatisation disorder most commonly presents with symptoms related to somatic organ systems, such as gastrointestinal, respiratory and cardiac.

stem: Mr Lewis is a 24-year-old man with a diagnosis of social phobia. He has been referred to your outpatient clinic for advice on medication, as he does not feel able to engage in psychological interventions at this time. Which of the following medications would be most likely to be benefi cial for him?
explanation: SSRIs are most commonly used in social phobia and have the best evidence base. Pregabalin is used for generalised anxiety disorder but does not have a suffi cient evidence base for social phobia. Clomipramine could be used for social phobia, but is not preferred; its main use is in OCD if an SSRI is ineff ective. Beta-blockers can be used for performance anxiety and can reduce physical symptoms of anxiety in a given situation but are not recommended for social phobia. Benzodiazepines can be used to manage severe anxiety but do not manage the underlying beliefs and are dependence-forming; they are not generally recommended.

stem: Miss Megan is a 39-year-old woman who has a history of presenting to various doctors, including GPs, out-of-hours services and private clinics. She is insistent that she has multiple sclerosis and that she is investigated for this despite there being no evidence of this during history taking or examination. When she is reassured that there is no reason for investigations and there is no evidence of MS she tends to become angry before leaving the clinic. Which of the following is most likely to be the diagnosis?
explanation: This is most likely to represent hypochondriasis. In this disorder an individual has an overvalued idea that they are ill, often with a specifi c disorder, and repeatedly presents to health services to confi rm this. They can be temporarily reassured in some cases, but can be irritable if healthcare staff s do not accede to their requests.

stem: Mr Powell is a 55-year-old man. He has been picked up by the police and taken to local Emergency Department as being found a substantial distance from his home with no memory of going there. There is no physical cause found for this and his concentration and cognition are intact on testing in the hospital. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This appears to represent a dissociative fugue whereby an individual, usually after encountering a stressor, will wander in the community until they are found or they come out of the fugue. They will have no memory of their travels although they may have appeared normal to those they encountered. Their cognition is usually normal once the episode has passed.

stem: Lithium is a highly eff ective medication for bipolar disorder, which must be maintained within a specifi c therapeutic range to prevent subtherapeutic levels or toxicity. Which of the following medications is most associated with neurotoxicity when prescribed with lithium?
explanation: Haloperidol,fl uphenazine andfl upenthixol have been associated with irreversible toxic encephalopathy when combined with lithium, and are particularly associated with neurotoxicity, even when lithium is within the therapeutic range.

stem: Mrs. Galsworthy is a 32-year-old woman with a diagnosis of OCD. She is currently under your care in an outpatient clinic and is due to start active treatment. She and her husband have asked about her likely prognosis. Which of the following is most associated with a positive prognosis in the short term in OCD?
explanation: An early and positive response to SSRI treatment is predictive of remission of OCD symptoms.

stem: Mrs. Vaughn is a 38-year-old woman with a diagnosis of epilepsy. She has recently presented to her GP with symptoms of low mood, inability to enjoy her usual activities and poor sleep. Which of the following is most likely to increase the risk of developing depression among people with epilepsy?
explanation: Complex partial seizures and absence of secondary generalized tonic–clonic seizures are risk factors for depression. Treatment with clonazepam, frequent hospitalizations (drug resistance) and lack of occupational activity are additional signifi cant contributing factors.

stem: Mr Howard Hughes is a 43-year-old man who has repeatedly attended his GP surgery and local A&E with concerns that something is blocking his throat. He has had numerous negative investigations, including direct visualisation of his pharynx, which can temporarily reassure him. Nevertheless, he continues to present himself. When asked, he describes a sense of something in his throat and is clearly very anxious. This is most likely to be
explanation: This is most likely to be hypochondriasis as the patient has an overvalued idea about a particular diagnosis. In somatisation disorder, patients describe numerous and often changeable physical symptoms. Patients experiencing psychotic symptoms would generally not be reassured, even temporarily, by negative investigationfi ndings. Note that DSM-5 prefers the term Somatic Symptom Disorder for the same presentation.

stem: Post-natal depression can lead to signifi cant distress in new mothers and impair their ability to bond with and care for their newborn children. What percentage of new mothers suff ers from postnatal depression?
explanation: It is thought that 10-15% of new mothers experience post-natal depression, with rates reducing to <10% after 12 weeks postpartum. Ref: Leahy-Warren et al., Arch Psychiatr Nurs. 2011 Jun;25(3):174-84

stem: Inpatient suicide rates in the UK have reduced signifi cantly since 2000. Which of the following is thought to have contributing most to this decrease?
options: Use of formal risk assessment tools
explanation: In the UK, hanging was the reported method in 77% of inpatient suicides between 1999 and 2007. The most common ligature points were doors, hooks or handles, windows, belts, and sheets or towels. Removal of ligature points had a signifi cant impact on the rate of inpatient suicides, though the use of shoelaces, doors, and windows increased over time. Ref; Bowers, L.; Dack, C.; Gul, N.; Thomas, B.; James, K. (2011) Learning from prevented suicide in psychiatric inpatient care: An analysis of data from the National Patient Safety Agency. International Journal of Nursing Studies 48 (12) 1459-1465

stem: People with schizophrenia can have certain cognitive impairments that are present when they are not experiencing an episode of psychosis. Which of the following is most common?
explanation: The most common cognitive impairments in schizophrenia are those around executive functioning and working memory.

stem: Mr Charlie Simms is a 26-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with schizophrenia. Once he has recovered he is keen to know more about his prognosis and what factors might have an impact on it. Which of the following factors is most likely to support a favourable prognosis?
correctAnswer: Family history of aff ective disorder
explanation: A family history of aff ective disorder is associated with a positive prognosis, as is having aff ective symptoms during episodes of illness. Acute onset, short duration of untreated symptoms, older age of onset, good premorbid functioning, being in a stable relationship and having a good support system are all positive prognostic factors in schizophrenia.

stem: Puerperal psychosis is a psychotic illness that tends to occur shortly after a woman gives birth. Which of the following is the most common presentation?
explanation: Prominent aff ective symptoms and unusual behaviour are the most common presenting symptoms in puerperal psychosis. This is often associated with profound anxiety and this can be associated with persecutory ideation. Many patients later satisfy the criteria for psychotic bipolar disorder.

stem: Mr Edward Hughes is a 23-year-old man with autism spectrum disorder and moderate intellectual impairment. He lives in a placement and has been demonstrating aggressive behaviour over the last several months. Attempts to identify the cause of his distress or address his behaviour via non-pharmacological methods have been fruitless. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for him?
explanation: Risperidone and Aripiprazole have the greatest evidence base for the pharmacological management of aggression in ASD. Other second- andfi rst-generation antipsychotics, antiepileptic medications, lithium, naltrexone and N-acetylcysteine have also been used although with less evidence being available for these agents.

stem: Mr Neil Peterson is a 36-year-old man who is currently experiencing a moderate depressive episode. He is struggling to motivate himself to engage with his usual activities and is due to be assessed for behavioural activation therapy. Which of the following will this include?
explanation: Assessment for behavioural activation therapy includes identifi cation of TRAP (Trigger, Response, Avoidance Pattern) with the avoidance including direct avoidance, rumination and use of alcohol, drugs and other maladaptive coping strategies. The aim is to replace this with TRAC (Trigger, Response, Alternate Coping response). Ref: Weinstock LM, Munroe MK, Miller IW. Behavioral activation for the treatment of atypical depression: a pilot open trial. Behavior modifi cation. 2011 Jul;35(4):403-24.

stem: Mrs Susan Matthews is a 42-year-old woman with a previous diagnosis of bipolar aff ective disorder. She has been well without medication for three years but has now presented with a clear-cut episode of depression. Which of the following would be most appropriate to treat her?
explanation: NICE recommends that individuals with a diagnosis of bipolar depression, who are not currently receiving medication, should be prescribed either Olanzapine and Fluoxetine in combo or Quetiapine by itself asfi rst line treatment. Patients can choose to have Olanzapine without Fluoxetine if desired (but not the antidepressant alone). Lamotrigine can also be off ered if the above therapies are ineff ective or the patient expresses a preference for it. Ref: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg185/

stem: ECT is a highly eff ective intervention in those with severe episodes of depression, which are treatment resistant or associated with risk to life. Which of the following is true about ECT?
options: A history of Ischemic heart disease is an absolute contraindication for ECT
An ECT-induced seizure lasting longer than 2 minutes should be pharmacologically aborted
Seizures on EEG last longer than the physical seizure
Antidepressants should be discontinued while ECT is delivered.
ECT can only be delivered for inpatients
correctAnswer: Seizures on EEG last longer than the physical seizure
explanation: It is common for seizure activity on the EEG to continue for longer than the physical movements, particularly as patients receiving ECT will have also have been administered a muscle relaxant. Ref: Fink M, Abrams R. EEG monitoring in ECT: a guide to treatment effi cacy. Psychiatric Times, May. 1998 May 1;15(5).

stem: Tina Keyes is a 2-year-old girl who was born with a cleft palate, which is in the process of being surgically repaired. She demonstrated evidence of development delay during herfi rst year and it is now thought that she will likely have a degree of intellectual disability. Which of the following medications taken during pregnancy is most likely to have contributed to these problems?
explanation: Sodium valproate should not be prescribed to women of childbearing age unless other therapies are ineff ective or inappropriate. If taken throughout pregnancy, about 10% of infants will have a congenital malformation and 40% will have a degree of developmental delay and intellectual impairment. Sertraline and other SSRIs are associated with a small increase in the risk of congenital malformations. Lithium was associated with an increase in the risk of congenital malformations, particularly Ebstein's anomaly. Benzodiazepines were considered to be associated with cleft lip and palate, but recent studies indicate that the risk is much lower than what was thought before. Antipsychotics, with the exception of risperidone, which shows a small increase in the risk of cardiac defects, are not associated with congenital abnormalities or developmental problems.

stem: Mr Vincent Payes is a 38-year-old man with a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia. He has had a recent relapse, which has been successfully treated with Olanzapine, but he reports that it makes him rather sedated during the day, including when he is driving. It appears likely that it is impairing his ability to drive. Which of the following should be done?
options: Report the patient's inability to drive to the DVLA directly
Advise the patient to omit the Olanzapine if they have to drive the next day
Advise the patient to stop driving and report to the DVLA themselves
Advise the patient to continue to drive but be cautious
correctAnswer: Advise the patient to stop driving and report to the DVLA themselves
explanation: The patient needs to stop driving if their medication may be impairing their ability to do so safely. It is usually appropriate to advise the patient to stop driving and inform the DVLA. It may then be appropriate to modify their prescription so they are not so sedated during the day, provided this does not compromise their mental wellbeing. If a patient will not inform the DVLA himself or herself, then it is appropriate to contact them directly. The patient's confi dentiality can be breached for this purpose.

stem: Abdominal pain is a common presenting symptom amongst children seen in paediatric practice. Which of the following is true regarding abdominal pain in children?
options: Abdominal pain in children usually responds readily to medical interventions
Abdominal pain is usually associated with clear bowel symptoms
Abdominal pain is a common symptom of anxiety in children
Abdominal pain related to anxiety in children is usually very well localised to one spot
Abdominal pain is usually associated with a persistent disturbance in appetite
correctAnswer: Abdominal pain is a common symptom of anxiety in children
explanation: Abdominal pain in children, whilst it can occasionally be due to signifi cant organic pathology, is usually ill defi ned and without clearly associated physical symptoms. It is commonly associated with anxiety and worry. Ref; Cunningham NR, et al. Importance of addressing anxiety in youth with functional abdominal pain: suggested guidelines for physicians. Journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition. 2013 May;56(5):469.

stem: Reading diffi culties are relatively common and aff ected children and adults may need certain adaptations to engage with education and work. What is the male: female ratio of reading diffi culties?
explanation: If reading diffi culties are defi ned as 2 standard deviations below mean, then the male: female ratio is 2:1. If 3 standard deviations are used, this increases to 4:1 due to the greater variance in male reading ability. Ref: Arnett AB, et al. Explaining the sex diff erence in dyslexia. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 2017 Jun;58(6):719-27.

stem: Anorexia nervosa most commonly aff ects females and is characterised by body image distortion and behaviours focused upon losing weight, most commonly in terms of dietary restriction but also excessive exercise and purging. When is it most likely to present?
explanation: The average age of onset of anorexia nervosa is 16-17 years.

stem: Sam Allen is a 10-year-old boy who has been referred to their local CAMHS clinic after it was noted that they were speaking at home but not at school. They are subsequently diagnosed with selective mutism. Which of the following is true regarding selective mutism?
options: Usually not associated with other mental disorder
It tends to entirely resolve over several months
explanation: Selective mutism is relatively rare, occurring in about 0.71% of children. It is highly associated with other anxiety disorders, particularly social phobia. It may be more common in girls than boys and tends to present between the ages of 3-6 years, when a child enters nursery or primary school. Children who recover tend to have ongoing social and talking diffi culties.

stem: Autism spectrum disorders are characterised by impairments in social interactions and communication and restricted and repetitive interests. They can also be associated with language delay and intellectual impairment. Which of the following is the greatest risk factor for the development of an autism spectrum disorder?
explanation: A low 5-minute APGAR score is associated with later ASD. Other perinatal risk factors for ASD are: abnormal presentation, umbilical-cord complications, foetal distress, birth injury or trauma, multiple birth, maternal hemorrhage, summer birth, low birth weight, small for gestational age, congenital malformation, feeding diffi culties, meconium aspiration, neonatal anemia, ABO or Rh incompatibility, and hyperbilirubinemia. Overalll, genetic factors are the greatest known risk factors for ASD. Ref; Modabbernia A, Sandin S, Gross R, Leonard H, Gissler M, Parner ET, Francis R, Carter K, Bresnahan M, Schendel D, Hornig M. Apgar score and risk of autism. European journal of epidemiology. 2018 Oct 5:1-0.

stem: Conduct disorder is a disorder seen in adolescents characterised by repeatedly defi ant and transgressing behaviour, often with aggression, rule breaking and other criminal behaviour. Which of the following is the most appropriatefi rst line intervention?
explanation: Parental psychoeducation and training is most eff ective in conduct disorder so they can eff ectively establish and maintain boundaries with the child and enable positive behavioural strategies to be enacted. Achieving behavioural change without clear boundaries and routines is very challenging.

stem: To explore the current practices and challenges in night-time care for people with dementia living in care homes in the UK, focus group discussions were held with care staff and family carers fromfi ve care homes in South London. Care home staff were recruited through the Maudsley Biomedical Research Centre Care Home Research Network in South London. Care home managers were asked to nominate members of staff to share their experiences of night-time care and sleep disturbance in people with dementia. Focus groups for care staff and family carers were conducted separately. Following focus groups, an online survey was circulated to 16 family carers to specifi cally explore the themes that emerged from focus groups. 19 informal interviews were also conducted with night-time care staff and nurses. Thematic analysis revealed eight key themes in the management of sleep disturbance in people with dementia living in care homes: current night-time care practices, dissonance in perceived causes of sleep disturbances, inconsistencies in treatment options, insuffi cient staffi ng levels, working relationships between shifts, nurse burden and responsibility, communication as a critical challenge, connecting with residents and one overarching theme of balance. The key themes identifi ed represent the major barriers to good quality care and areas which future programmes will need to address to improve the quality of night-time care in care homes (Nunez et al., Int J Geriatr Psychiatry. 2018;33(1):e140-e149). In this study, focus groups for care staff and family carers were conducted separately. Which if the following is the most likely reason for this decision?
options: To allow participants to freely express themselves
To complete the study within the stipulated time
To allow thematic analysis of the data
correctAnswer: To allow participants to freely express themselves
explanation: For a focus group methodology to be productive, we may need to categorize our participants by relevant demographic or qualitative experience based variables whichever is relevant for the questions under consideration. This ensures that the groups are homogenous, and allows free expression of views. Ref: Smithson J. Using and analysing focus groups: limitations and possibilities. International journal of social research methodology. 2000 Jan 1;3(2):103-19.

stem: Choe et al. tested the performance of the combined use of CAGE and GGT to screen alcohol dependence (AD). (Choe YM, et al. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. 2019;15:1507).Which of the following screening procedures is likely to have the largest area under the ROC curve?
explanation: The area under a ROC curve is larger for crives that are closer to the vertex than to the chance line. Among the given curves, the curve for AUDIT is the closest to the vertex and farthest from the chance line. This means that the discrimination accuracy for AUDIT is likely to be much better than that can be achieved by a random coin toss to diagnose alcohol dependence.

stem: Choe et al. tested the performance of the combined use of CAGE and GGT to screen alcohol dependence (AD). (Choe YM, et al. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. 2019;15:1507). Which of the following screening procedures is likely to have the least discrimination accuracy for identifying alcohol dependence?

explanation: Fagan's nomogram, also called Bayes' nomogram, helps us to quantify the post-test probability that an individual is aff ected by a condition given an observed test result and given the probability of the individual having the condition before the test was run (pretest probability or prevalence). To use the Fagan's nomogram (as depicted in the providedfi gure), we must draw a straight line from the provided pretest probability on the left column through the likelihood ratio (LR+ or LR-) in the middle column; the intersection of our line with the right column provides the required post-test probability values. options: Accuracy of the test has changed
The test performs poorly in certain situations
The likelihood ratio varies with the sample
Predictive values are heavily dependent on prevalence
correctAnswer: Predictive values are heavily dependent on prevalence
explanation: The sensitivity and specifi city of a test are test characteristics that can vary with the cut-off , but not with the prevalence of the disease (i.e. pre-test probability does not aff ect these values). Consequently, the Likelihood Ratio, which are mathematically derived from sensitivity and specifi city, also are not aff ected by prevalence. However, the positive and negative predictive values (i.e. post-test probabilities) are aff ected by the sensitivity, specifi city as well as the prevalence of the disease in the population that is being studied. Ref: Trevethan R. Sensitivity, specifi city, and predictive values: foundations, pliabilities, and pitfalls in research and practice. Frontiers in public health. 2017 Nov 20;5:307.

She uses proportion of eligible patients on antipsychotic prescriptions for whom HbA1c measurements are not available at various clinics as the benchmark and generates the following plot. This plot is best termed as
explanation: Funnel plots show the observed performance (using a specifi c variable) of individual clinics in reference to a benchmark standard. The estimated performance marker (proportion of patients with recorded HbA1c) is plotted against of the precision of the measurement (in this case, no. of clinic visits). The control limits form a "funnel" shape such that if an observed clinic/institution falls outside the limits, the divergence is used as a marker for further action. Ref: Verburg IW, et al. Guidelines on constructing funnel plots for quality indicators: A case study on mortality in intensive care unit patients. Statistical methods in medical research. 2018 Nov;27(11):3350-66.

She uses proportion of eligible patients on antipsychotic prescriptions for whom HbA1c measurements are not available at various clinics as the benchmark and generates the following plot. The purpose of this plot is
options: Identify the relationship between quantity and quality of clinical performance in each clinic
To enable detection of outlier status
Visualisation of factors contributing to poor performance
correctAnswer: To enable detection of outlier status
explanation: In quality improvement studies such as audits, funnel plots are used as tools to compare clinical performance of a group of professionals or institutions on a quality indicator against a benchmark. By providing a visual indication of "divergent" performance they enable detection of outliers that require remedial actions to improve their performance. These plots do not provide causal explanations for poor performance, and do not indicate if the volume of work relates to the quality of work within an institution. Unlike the funnel plots used for meta-analysis, we cannot infer any reporting or publication bias from these plots. Ref: Spiegelhalter, DJ . Handling over-dispersion of performance indicators. Qual Saf Health Care 2005; 14: 347–351.

stem: An observational study was undertaken with linkage of nationwide registers of all people with a diagnosis of bipolar disorder in psychiatric hospital settings who were prescribed valproate or lithium in Denmark during a period from 1995 to 2006. A total of 4268 participants were included among whom 719 received valproate and 3549 received lithium subsequent to the diagnosis of bipolar disorder. Cumulative incidence for the risks of interest was estimated for the total population accounting for the competing risks. The rate of psychiatric hospital admissions was increased for valproate v. lithium (HR = 1.33, 95% CI 1.18–1.48) and regardless of the type of episode leading to a hospital admission (depressive or manic/mixed). Similarly, for participants with a depressive index episode (HR=1.87, 95% CI 1.40–2.48), a manic index episode (HR = 1.24, 95% CI 1.01–1.51) and a mixed index episode (HR = 1.44, 95% CI 1.04–2.01), the overall rate of hospital admissions was signifi cantly increased for valproate compared with lithium. The authors concluded that in daily clinical practice, treatment with lithium is likely to be superior to treatment with valproate for bipolar disorder. Kessing LV, et al.. The British Journal of Psychiatry. 2011 Jul;199(1):57- 63. What type of study is this?
explanation: This is a retrospective cohort study. The exposure is lithium and valproate. It is a pharmaco-epidemiological study based on observational data; not a controlled trial.

explanation: Both Kaplan Meier survival curve and a cumulative incidence curve can be derived from survival tables. As opposed to Kaplan-Meier survival curves that show the probability of surviving an event over time, the cumulative incidence curve shows the probabilities of experiencing the event of interest. At any given time, cumulative incidence is [1- the proportion surviving past the time interval t]. While a Kaplan-Meier curve steps down with time towards the bottom, a cumulative incidence curve steps up towards the top. One of the limitations with Kaplan Meier approach is that it can handle only one single event at a time (e.g. hospital admission): all other events (death, change of diagnosis, change of treatment etc.) are treated as censored observations and the complement of the Kaplan–Meier estimate (1-KM) is interpreted as the probability of the event of interest. In other words, KM approach assumes that competing events infl uencing the outcome does not exist, which is far from reality. In clinical practice, patients who experience a competing event (e.g. treatment change such as addition of an antipsychotic to lithium) often have a very diff erent probability of survival for the event of interest (i.e. hospital admission in this case). As a result, the Kaplan–Meier method is considered to be less conservative (i.e. it often overestimates the outcome probability) and not valid when competing risks are present. In such situations, it is preferable to use a cumulative incidence function that adjusts for competing as in this study. Excerpts from Noordzij M, et al.. Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation. 2013 Nov 1;28(11):2670-7.

stem: Prospectively gathered nationwide databases were linked to study the risk of rehospitalization and treatment failure in relation to antipsychotic treatments for patients with schizophrenia, from July 1, 2006, to December 31, 2013, among all patients in Sweden with a schizophrenia diagnosis who were 16 to 64 years of age in 2006 (29?823 patients in the total prevalent cohort; 4603 in the incident cohort of newly diagnosed patients). Risk of rehospitalization and treatment failure (defi ned as psychiatric rehospitalization, suicide attempt, discontinuation or switch to other medication, or death) were the main outcome measures. The risk of psychiatric rehospitalization was the lowest during monotherapy with once-monthly long-acting injectable paliperidone (hazard ratio [HR], 0.51; 95% CI, 0.41-0.64), long-acting injectable zuclopenthixol (HR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.48-0.57), clozapine (HR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.48-0.58) compared with no use of antipsychotic medication. Clozapine (HR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.53-0.63) and all long-acting injectable antipsychotic medications (HRs 0.65-0.80) were associated with the lowest rates of treatment failure compared with the most widely used medication, oral olanzapine. Clozapine and long-acting injectable antipsychotic medications were the pharmacologic treatments with the highest rates of prevention of relapse in schizophrenia. The risk of rehospitalization is about 20% to 30% lower during long-acting injectable treatments compared with equivalent oral formulations. Tiihonen J, et al. JAMA psychiatry. 2017 Jul 1;74(7):686-93.

JAMA psychiatry. 2017 Jul 1;74(7):686-93. 16. Which of the following is the most important bias aff ecting this study design?
explanation: People with diff erent baseline prognostic factors often get systematically selected for certain treatments e.g. suicidal patients for clozapine, noncompliant patients for depot injections. In pharmaco-epidemiological observations, this can lead to a "channelling bias" whereby the treatments may appear to be related to the outcomes, while in fact, the outcomes relate to the diff erences in the profi les of patient groups selected for the treatments. Another related bias specifi c to pharmaco-epidemiological studies is confounding by indication or 'indication bias'. This occurs when the reason for a prescription (e.g. clozapine use, depot injection use) is associated with the outcome of interest (relapse, rehospitalisation), rather than the medication itself infl uencing the outcome. These 2 biases can be mitigated by undertaking within-individual comparisons (i.e. between each treatment trial for the same patient during the 6.9 years median observation period). As each patient served as his/her own control, the channelling bias and indication bias are likely to be attenuated, though residual confounding cannot be ruled out. In pharmaco-epidemiology, another common fallacy is one of reverse causality or protopathic bias. A particular treatment may be initiated because of the outcome event, not the other way around. This bias might have favoured the periods with no antipsychotic use. Excerpts from Faillie, J. Br J Clin Pharmacol. 2015 Oct; 80(4): 779–780; Rubio JM, Correll CU. A study can report results that are statistically signifi cant, but this may not be clinically signifi cant, i.e. a small eff ect that wont make perceptible change for the patient or the practitioner. It is also possible for clinically signifi cant changes to not reach the threshold for statistical signifi cance. Such clinically important diff erences may still be valuable when considering treatment recommendations. Ref: Page, Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2014 Oct; 9(5): 726–736.

stem: What is a systematic error?
options: An error leading to a false positive inference
A type of error present in all studies with the same sample
An error leading to acceptance of null hypothesis
An error in measurement made each time
correctAnswer: An error in measurement made each time
explanation: Systematic errors are consistent errors, which occur with each measurement, thus have a high likelihood of occurring again when we repeat the experiment. They are not random errors. Bias is one type of systematic error that leads to an incorrect estimate of association, thus resulting in either a false positive or false negative inference.

stem: A 40-year-old man is a long term cocaine user. He is likely to have abnormalities in which of the following cognitive domains?
explanation: Being a stimulant, cocaine enhances cognitive functions, especially response inhibition and psychomotor processing speed, acutely after administration, though long-term use impairs cognition. 30% of dependent users and even 12% of recreational users exhibit clinically relevant cognitive impairment (see Vonmoos et al., 2014). The most impaired domains were sustained attention, response inhibition (impulsivity), verbal learning/memory, and working memory (Spronk et al., 2013). Abstinence helps to attain a level of cognitive performance level similar to non-users. Such recovery of cognition is not complete, as working memory impairments may continue despite 1-year of abstinence, especially in those who start cocaine use at an early age (Vonmoos et al., 2014).

stem: Which of the following substance, even when used concurrently with clozapine, does not aff ect the metabolism of clozapine?
explanation: Dose adjustments are often necessary when certain medications are used concurrently with clozapine. CYP1A2 inhibitors (e.g.,fl uvoxamine or ciprofl oxacin [strong], oral contraceptives or caff eine [moderate]); CYP2D6 or CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., escitalopram, erythromycin, paroxetine, bupropion,fl uoxetine, duloxetine [moderate], sertraline or diazepam [weak]) can increase adverse eff ects associated with clozapine's by aff ecting its breakdown. With strong inhibitors, it is advisable to initiate with one-third of the usual clozapine dose and titrate slowly. If these ' CYP inhibitors' are discontinued during clozapine treatment, then clozapine dose must be increased; else its therapeutic eff ectiveness could be lost. CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine, St. John's wort, and rifampin) or CYP1A2 inducers (e.g., tobacco smoking) can increase clozapine metabolism and thus reduce eff ectiveness. If these agents are used, clozapine dose should be increased to achieve the same therapeutic eff ect. If these are discontinued during clozapine treatment, then clozapine dose must be reduced, else dose-related adverse eff ects associated with clozapine will become more pronounced. Please note that it is the tar in cigarettes that induce CYP1A2 activity, not nicotine. Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) does not usually aff ect clozapine levels.
